item.title: Coding with an AI agent: Claude Code in Positron
item.dc:creator: Jelmer Poelstra
item.description:
1 Introduction

1.1 What we’ll cover

In the previous session, we used AI through Posit Assistant and GitHub Copilot in Positron to help you make plots. Today, we’ll use a different kind of AI tool: Claude Code, Anthropic’s “agentic” coding tool, which we’ll run inside Positron.

We’ll start small, by having Claude write a script for a single plot, and work our way up to tasks that would take you quite a while by yourself: cleaning up a messy dataset, writing a Quarto report with plots and nicely formatted tables, giving it Ohio State branding, and building a small Shiny app. Specifically, we’ll cover:

  • Setting up Claude Code in Positron with an OSU API key
  • Having Claude write, run, and check R code
  • Giving Claude your files as context
  • Stopping, steering, and rewinding Claude while it works
  • Persistent instructions with a CLAUDE.md file
  • A mini-project: from a messy CSV to a branded Quarto report and a Shiny app

The appendix covers managing context and cost, good habits when working with an agent, and a bonus exercise in which Claude finds and fixes bugs.

We picked these tasks because they are a sweet spot for AI help: hard to write, but easy to check. Polished tables, interactive plots, and Shiny apps take a lot of code, using packages and syntax that most of us don’t use often enough to remember. But you can tell at a glance whether a plot, a table, or an app looks and works the way you want. Compare this with, say, a statistical analysis, where code can run without errors and still give subtly wrong results that are hard to spot.

1.2 From chat to agents

When you use AI through a browser-based chat, the model can’t see your files unless you paste or upload them, and it can’t check whether the code it writes actually works. AI agents, on the other hand, can work inside your editor and:

  • Read the files in your project, so you don’t have to explain or paste them
  • Edit and create files, showing you each change for approval
  • Run code and commands, and then look at the results, including errors and even the plots they made
  • Hack HuggingFace 😱

1.3 Posit Assistant vs. Claude Code

Posit Assistant, which we used in the previous session, is also an agent. In fact, it has a key built-in strength that Claude Code does not have: it is connected to your live R session, so it can see your objects and run code in your console1.

On the other hand, Claude Code has the edge in other areas:

  • It is a general-purpose coding agent and is designed also with longer-running, multi-step tasks in mind.
  • It is a more mature product overall. For example, we’ve had authentication problems with Posit Assistant, both via GitHub and with an API key, but not with Claude Code.

(Claude Code also comes in other forms, like a command-line program and a desktop app. Here, we’ll use its VS Code extension in Positron.)

1.4 Authentication with an API key

Rather than using a personal account, we’ll authenticate through an API key from OSU’s Generative AI Service , which is approved for use with restricted institutional data (S2–S4)2. We’ll give you a personal API key for this session with limited credit.

If you’d like to continue using Claude Code or Posit Assistant in this manner after today’s Code Club, you’ll have to set this up via the link above — but keep in mind that it isn’t free, so your PI (or similar) would need to have funds that can be used for this purpose.

Alternatively (or additionally), you could get a personal Anthropic subscription. Per token, this is a lot cheaper than usage with an API key, but you’ll need to pay personally and you shouldn’t use it with institutional data.

NoteLearn more

Parts of this session are adapted from my PLNTPTH 5006 (“Practical Computing Skills for Omics Data”) course material, which is publicly available (weeks 8 and 9 cover genAI).

The lecture slides cover the use of Generative AI in research and coding more broadly, whereas the practical part focuses on using Claude Code in VS Code for Unix shell scripting tasks. There are also links to further resources and pages on GitHub Copilot and more advanced Claude Code features.

2 Getting set up

2.1 First installations

If you haven’t done so already, please:

  1. Install Positron and R version 4.5.0 or higher — see the Positron session for details. (We’ll use the penguins data that is built into R since version 4.5.0.)

  2. Install Quarto. Positron comes with its own copy of Quarto, but Claude can’t find that copy when it runs commands, so it needs a regular Quarto installation to render documents.

  3. Install the R packages we’ll use:

    install.packages("tidyverse")
install.packages("gt")
install.packages("shiny")
install.packages("bslib")

    We’ll leave a few other packages that Claude will likely want to use uninstalled (countrycode, gtExtras, and ggiraph), so you can see how Claude asks before installing packages.

NoteWindows users: Git for Windows (optional) (Click to expand)

On Windows, Claude Code runs commands with PowerShell by default. If you have Git for Windows installed, it will use Git Bash instead, which is what it does on Mac and Linux. Both work for today, so there’s no need to install Git for Windows just for this session.

2.2 Download and open the project folder

  1. Download this zip file and unzip it. You may want to move the resulting codeclub-claude folder into a folder for Code Club, e.g. Documents/codeclub/codeclub-claude.

  2. Open the codeclub-claude folder in Positron with File > Open Folder..., and trust the folder when asked.

The folder contains the following files:

codeclub-claude
├── factbook.csv        # World Bank data from the previous session
└── penguin_summary.R   # A script with some problems...

Claude treats the folder that is open in Positron as its “workspace”: this is where it will look for files, and by default the only place where it can make changes.

2.3 Install the Claude Code extension

  1. In the Extensions view in the Activity Bar, search for “claude”, and click Install for the extension “Claude Code for VS Code” by Anthropic.

  2. If asked whether you trust the publisher “Anthropic”, click Trust Publisher & Install.

2.4 Connect Claude to your API key

To tell Claude to use your API key, you need a settings file called settings.json in a folder .claude in your Home folder. Claude reads this file every time it starts up.

Let’s set this up:

  1. Create the folder and the (empty) file, and open the file in the editor, by copying the code below into the Positron console and pressing Enter 3:

    # Get your Home folder (on Windows, R's "~" points to Documents instead)
home <- if (.Platform$OS.type == "windows") {
  Sys.getenv("USERPROFILE")
} else {
  path.expand("~")
}

# Create the .claude folder and the settings file
# (an existing settings file is left alone)
settings_file <- file.path(home, ".claude", "settings.json")
dir.create(dirname(settings_file), showWarnings = FALSE)
if (!file.exists(settings_file)) file.create(settings_file)

# Open the file in the editor
file.edit(settings_file)

  2. Paste the following contents into the file that opened in the editor:

    ~/.claude/settings.json
    {
  "env": {
    "ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL": "https://litellm.cloud.osu.edu",
    "ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN": "API-KEY",
    "ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL": "claude-opus-5-5",
    "ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_SONNET_MODEL": "claude-sonnet-5",
    "ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_HAIKU_MODEL": "claude-haiku-5-5",
    "CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_EXPERIMENTAL_BETAS": "1"
  },
  "model": "sonnet",
  "effortLevel": "medium",
  "outputStyle": "Concise",
  "theme": "auto"
}

  3. Replace the placeholder API-KEY with your personal API key as shown below, and save the file:

    ~/.claude/settings.json (excerpt - with fictional API key)
        "ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN": "bY-7jiuWbfck9DZk34hA_t",
NoteMore about the settings file (Click to expand)

The file is in JSON format, a plain-text format with key-value pairs: a colon : separates each key from its value, pairs are separated by commas, and curly braces {} group pairs. A single missing quote or comma breaks the whole file (this would be a likely culprit if Claude doesn’t pick up your API key).

  • ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL makes Claude go through OSU’s service rather than directly to Anthropic.
  • ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN is the API key.
  • The MODEL lines specify which model versions to use.
  • CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_EXPERIMENTAL_BETAS turns off experimental features that OSU’s service doesn’t support, and that would otherwise cause errors.
  • model and effortLevel set the default model (Sonnet) and effort level (Medium).
  • outputStyle makes Claude’s answers shorter and more to the point (remove this line if you prefer longer explanations).
  • theme makes Claude’s colors follow your computer’s light or dark mode.
ImportantTreat the API key like a password (Click to expand)

Anyone with your key can use it, and usage costs money and depletes your key’s budget. So never share your key or commit it to a Git repository. That’s one reason the settings file is located in your Home folder, and not in a project folder that others may see.

2.5 Open Claude

Open Claude Code by clicking the Claude icon at the top of the secondary (right-hand) side bar — the one with the blue line under it in the screenshot below:

TipAlternatively, open it in the editor pane (Click to expand)

You can also click the orange Claude icon in the top-right corner of the editor. This opens Claude as a tab in the editor, which has two potential advantages:

  • You can have multiple Claude tabs, i.e. multiple conversations, open at the same time, instead of having to switch between conversations in the same tab.

  • You don’t have to switch back and forth between Claude and the Variables, Plots, and Help panes, which share the secondary side bar.

On the other hand, things can get a bit more chaotic with Claude as a tab, and it has less vertical space than the secondary side bar.

In the Claude panel, you may initially see various login options (left screenshot below), but if you simply wait, Claude should read your settings file, and you should see a prompt box at the bottom of the Claude tab (right screenshot below):

To check that Claude works, type the following prompt in the box and press Enter:

Write a horoscope for a dataset with 40% missing values

If you get a horoscope back, Claude is set up correctly.

If you get an error instead, or Claude merely keeps printing verbs like “Brewing” and “Deliberating” (Claude’s variant on a spinning wheel) but nothing else, let us know, and we’ll help you troubleshoot.

3 Basics of the interface

The buttons across the bottom of the prompt box are, from left to right:

  • + adds files as context to your prompt.

  • / opens the command menu, with nearly all of Claude Code’s options and settings.

  • A clock icon with a number of minutes appears once Claude has responded (see the section on cost).

  • Sonnet 5 Medium is the current model and effort level. Keep it at that, and don’t select “Default (recommended)”, which switches to the much more expensive Opus model.

  • Manual is the current permission mode (what Claude is allowed to do without asking you first).

At the top of the Claude tab, there are buttons to see your previous conversations (clock icon) and to start a new conversation (chat icon with a +). We’ll start a new conversation for each new task — you’ll see why later.

NotePermission modes (Click to expand)

Click on the permission mode to switch between modes:

  • Manual: Claude asks permission for each file edit and for most commands (it runs simple read-only commands without asking).
  • Edit automatically: Claude edits files without asking, but asks about running commands.
  • Auto: a separate AI model checks each action, and Claude only asks you about risky ones.
  • Plan: Claude only writes a plan, which you can review and modify before Claude carries it out. We’ll try this in the mini-project.

We’ll stick to Manual mode for most of today: it’s slower-going, but you’ll see exactly what Claude does. Once you’re comfortable reviewing Claude’s work, the many permission requests can become tedious, and it’s easy to start clicking “Yes” without reading what you approve. At that point, Auto mode is a good alternative.

4 A first example: a script for a single plot

4.1 Ask Claude to write a script

Start a new conversation, and submit the following prompt:

Write a script penguin_plot.R that makes a simple scatterplot of flipper length vs. body mass for R’s built-in penguins data, colored by species. It should print the plot and save it to penguins.png.

Claude will show you what it’s doing as it goes, and will ask you for permission to create the script, showing you its proposed contents. Take a quick look and accept it.

Next, it may want to run the script to check that it works, using a command like Rscript penguin_plot.R. Rscript is a way to run an R script from the terminal rather than from the console. Click Yes to let it run the command. (On Windows, if Claude can’t find Rscript, see this box.)

Finally, it will print some kind of summary of what it’s done:

You should see penguins.png in the file explorer on the left, and can click on it to view it. Here’s the plot I got:

Now, let’s ask it to improve the plot, in the same conversation:

Look at the plot you saved and suggest three improvements, then make them

Claude will propose to make changes and present you with a “diff”, where deletions are highlighted in red and additions in green4:

Once you’ve approved its requests to edit the file and running the script, look back at what is printed in the panel. You should see that Claude read the PNG file and looked at it before suggesting improvements: it can “see” images. (More broadly, this is a big difference from chat-based AI: Claude can check its own work, and iterate on it.)

Here’s what mine changed in a test-run:

Did you get similar changes? And here’s the resulting plot:

Let’s also take a look at the code in the script. Is there anything you find striking or that you don’t understand? Is your code substantially different from mine?

  Click to see the code I got 
penguin_plot.R
library(ggplot2)

# `penguins` is built into R (datasets package) as of R 4.5.0
n_complete <- sum(complete.cases(penguins[, c("body_mass", "flipper_len")]))

p <- ggplot(penguins, aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len, color = species, shape = species)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.7, na.rm = TRUE) +
  scale_color_viridis_d(option = "D", end = 0.85) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(
    x = "Body mass (g)",
    y = "Flipper length (mm)",
    color = "Species",
    shape = "Species",
    title = "Penguin flipper length vs. body mass",
    subtitle = paste0("n = ", n_complete, " penguins with complete measurements")
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

print(p)
ggsave("penguins.png", p, width = 6, height = 4, dpi = 300)

Let’s try one more:

Make it look like a chart from The Economist

Here’s the plot I got:

  Click to see the code I got 
penguin_plot.R
library(ggplot2)
library(grid)

# `penguins` is built into R (datasets package) as of R 4.5.0
n_complete <- sum(complete.cases(penguins[, c("body_mass", "flipper_len")]))

# Economist-style palette and background
econ_bg <- "#D9E6EB"
econ_red <- "#E3120B"
econ_colors <- c(Adelie = "#006BA2", Chinstrap = "#E3120B", Gentoo = "#EBB434")

p <- ggplot(penguins, aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len, color = species, shape = species)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.2, alpha = 0.85, na.rm = TRUE) +
  scale_color_manual(values = econ_colors) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(
    x = "Body mass (g)",
    y = "Flipper length (mm)",
    title = "Big feet, big birds",
    subtitle = "Flipper length v body mass of penguins, by species",
    caption = paste0("Source: Palmer Station LTER; n = ", n_complete, " penguins"),
    color = NULL,
    shape = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = econ_bg, color = NA),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = econ_bg, color = NA),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(color = "white", linewidth = 0.6),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    axis.line.x = element_line(color = "black", linewidth = 0.6),
    axis.ticks.x = element_line(color = "black", linewidth = 0.4),
    axis.ticks.length.x = unit(4, "pt"),
    axis.text = element_text(color = "grey25"),
    axis.title = element_text(color = "grey25", size = 9),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 15, margin = margin(b = 2)),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, margin = margin(b = 8)),
    plot.caption = element_text(color = "grey35", size = 8, hjust = 0),
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    plot.caption.position = "plot",
    legend.position = "top",
    legend.justification = "left",
    legend.text = element_text(size = 10),
    plot.margin = margin(22, 14, 8, 10)
  )

# Draw the plot plus the Economist's red tag in the top-left corner
draw_plot <- function() {
  print(p)
  grid.rect(
    x = 0, y = 1, width = unit(0.07, "npc"), height = unit(0.012, "npc"),
    just = c("left", "top"), gp = gpar(fill = econ_red, col = NA)
  )
}

draw_plot()
png("penguins.png", width = 6, height = 4, units = "in", res = 300)
draw_plot()
invisible(dev.off())
ImportantClaude runs its own R

Claude does not use the R session in your Positron console. When it runs a script, it starts a separate R process with Rscript, which means that:

  • Its plots don’t appear in your Plots pane, and the objects it creates don’t appear in your Variables pane.
  • It can’t see objects you created in the console. Anything it needs should be in a script or a file.

To see the results in Positron, simply run the script yourself.

5 File context, and interrupting Claude

5.1 Giving Claude your files as context

A key advantage of using AI inside your editor is that your files are readily available. Your entire workspace (the folder you opened in Positron) is “implicit” context: when Claude thinks it’s useful, it will search and read files there by itself.

But when you have specific files in mind, it’s often better to point Claude to them explicitly. That’s faster and cheaper, and avoids Claude guessing which files you mean:

  • The file that’s active in the editor is added automatically: you can see its name below the prompt box5.
  • You can also select specific lines in the active file, to focus Claude’s attention on them.
  • Type @ followed by part of a file name to add any file in your workspace.
  • To add multiple files, type @ for each, or press Alt/Option+K with a file active in the editor.

5.2 Stopping, steering, and rewinding

Sometimes you need to adjust what Claude is doing while it’s working:

  • Steer it: type a new message while Claude is working, and it will take that into account after a few seconds. (It helps to keep an eye on Claude’s intermediate messages!)
  • Stop it: press Esc or click the stop button.
  • Rewind: press Esc twice in quick succession, or hover over an earlier message and click the rewind button, to go back to an earlier point in the conversation and optionally undo file changes. (Claude is also good at undoing things when you simply ask it to.)

6 Persistent instructions with CLAUDE.md

6.1 Persistent instructions: why and how

Each new conversation with Claude starts from scratch: it doesn’t see what you discussed in earlier conversations. So you may find yourself repeatedly telling it the same things, such as “never modify the raw data”, “use the native pipe”, or “don’t use setwd()”.

Instead, you can put these kinds of instructions in a file called CLAUDE.md, a Markdown file that Claude automatically reads at the start of every conversation in your project (if you’re not familiar with Markdown, you can simply consider it a plain text file when you write in it). There is no required structure for its contents, but it should be concise and easy to read, for you as well as for Claude.

As a first example, create a new file CLAUDE.md in your project folder, add the following line to it, and save it:

CLAUDE.md
- Always answer like an overexcited sports commentator

Then, close the file (because any active file would be added to the prompt anyway, even if it wasn’t a CLAUDE.md file!), start a new conversation, and ask:

What’s the difference between <- and = in R?

6.2 Our instructions for this project

Replace the sports commentator line with the following:

CLAUDE.md
## R conventions

- Use paths relative to the project folder, and never use `setwd()`
- Use the tidyverse and the native pipe `|>`
- I'm an intermediate R user: prefer readable over clever code,
  and briefly explain non-obvious steps in comments
- Test R code by running it with `Rscript`, and Quarto documents with `quarto render`
- Ask before installing R packages
- Don't run Shiny apps yourself, since they keep running: I will run them

We’re leaving out any information about our data here, so we can see what Claude figures out by itself in the mini-project below. In a real research project, though, it’s worth adding sections that briefly describe your data files, your project’s file structure, and so on. As another example, you may want all your plots to have a certain theme, or to use a certain color palette, and you can put that in CLAUDE.md too.

Close the file again, and to check that Claude picks up the new instructions, start a new conversation and ask:

What rules should you follow in this project?

The response I got is in the screenshot on the right.

We’ll see these instructions in action in the mini-project below.

ImportantWindows users: tell Claude where Rscript is (Click to expand)

On Windows, R’s installer doesn’t make Rscript available to commands run outside of R, so Claude may struggle to find it. To help it, run the following in the Positron console:

normalizePath(file.path(R.home("bin"), "Rscript.exe"), winslash = "/")

And add the resulting path to the “R conventions” section of your CLAUDE.md, e.g.:

CLAUDE.md (excerpt)
- Rscript is at `C:/Program Files/R/R-4.5.1/bin/Rscript.exe`
NoteMore on using CLAUDE.md (Click to expand)

Drafting a CLAUDE.md with /init
Instead of writing a CLAUDE.md from scratch, you can type /init in the prompt box: Claude then looks through your project and drafts a CLAUDE.md for you to review and edit. This can be a useful start in a larger existing project, but the most valuable parts of a CLAUDE.md are things only you know: what the project is about, where the data is, and how you want things done.

Keep updating your CLAUDE.md
Start simple, and add to it whenever you notice yourself telling Claude the same thing again, or Claude making the same mistake again. Keep it short, though: it’s read at the start of every conversation, so it uses up tokens (and money) each time.

Instructions are not strict rules
Claude will usually but not always follow the instructions in CLAUDE.md.

Claude’s memory
Claude also keeps memory notes for itself: when you correct it or tell it about your preferences, it may save a note, which is loaded into future conversations in the same project. Type /memory in the prompt box to see and edit these.

7 Mini-project: from a messy CSV to a report and an app

We’ll work with the “factbook” data from the previous session, World Bank data that is now in factbook.csv. We’ll have Claude clean it, and then build a report and an app on top of the cleaned data.

7.1 A quick look at the data

First, let’s take a quick look at the data: click on factbook.csv in the Explorer pane to open it in the Data Explorer.

Scroll around, including to the bottom of the file, and you’ll see a few things that make the data awkward to work with:

  • It is in a “wide” format, with one column per year.
  • The year column names, like 2000 [YR2000], are not just numbers.
  • The year columns are text rather than numbers, because missing values are coded as ...
  • The last rows are not data, but empty rows and notes about the database.

Let’s see how Claude handles this.

We’ll start a new conversation for each step below. Thanks to the CLAUDE.md file and the files Claude creates along the way, it doesn’t need to remember the previous conversation.

7.2 Clean the data

Write clean-factbook.R that reads factbook.csv and saves a tidy version to factbook_tidy.csv with columns country, country_code, indicator, year (numeric), and value. Check the result.

Some things to watch for in its reply, the code, and the resulting factbook_tidy.csv:

  • How does Claude look at the data before writing code?
  • Did it figure out the .. missing values and the odd year column names by itself?
  • Did it notice the notes at the bottom of the file, which aren’t data? (Check the last rows of the tidy file.)
  • How did it “check the result”?
  • Is the code clear and does it have explanatory comments?

Let’s ask for one follow-up change:

Add a continent column

It’s likely that Claude will want to use the countrycode package to do this, and following our CLAUDE.md instructions, it will ask for permission to install the package first:

Let’s take another quick look at the data in the Data Explorer, to see if the continent column looks right.

  Click to see the final version of the script I got 
clean-factbook.R
library(tidyverse)
library(countrycode)

# Read everything as character first, because the `..` missing-value
# code would otherwise turn the year columns into text anyway
factbook <- read_csv("factbook.csv", col_types = cols(.default = "c"))

factbook_tidy <- factbook |>
  # The file ends with blank and footnote rows that have no country: remove them
  filter(!is.na(`Country Code`)) |>
  # Drop the series code; keep the readable indicator name
  select(
    country = `Country Name`,
    country_code = `Country Code`,
    indicator = `Series Name`,
    starts_with("20")
  ) |>
  # Wide -> long: one row per country x indicator x year
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("20"),
    names_to = "year",
    values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    # Column names look like "2000 [YR2000]": keep the first 4 characters
    year = as.numeric(str_sub(year, 1, 4)),
    # `..` marks missing values: turn into NA, then convert to numbers
    value = as.numeric(na_if(value, "..")),
    # Look up the continent from the ISO3 country code; Kosovo (XKX) and the
    # Channel Islands (CHI) have no standard match, so we set them manually
    continent = countrycode(
      country_code,
      origin = "iso3c",
      destination = "continent",
      custom_match = c(XKX = "Europe", CHI = "Europe")
    ),
    .after = country_code
  )

write_csv(factbook_tidy, "factbook_tidy.csv")

7.3 A Quarto report with gt tables

The gt package (“grammar of tables”) lets you build tables from data frames, much like ggplot2 does for plots. A report with nicely formatted tables is a good example of a “hard to write, easy to check” task. Things like color-coded cells or a small trend plot in each row of a gt table take many lines of code with options you’d probably have to look up every time, but one look at the rendered table tells you whether it worked.

This is a bigger task, so we’ll first ask Claude for a plan. Start a new conversation, click on the permission mode, and select Plan mode. Then, submit:

Create a Quarto report report.qmd that summarizes how countries changed between 2000 and 2015, using factbook_tidy.csv. Include 3-4 ggplot figures, a gt table of the 10 countries with the largest growth in GDP per capita, with color-coded cells and a small plot of the trend in each row, and a short narrative for each section. Make the plots and table attractive but also readable. Render the report to HTML and fix any errors.

Claude will explore the files and then present a plan as a Markdown document. Take a look at the plan. For example, how did Claude interpret “largest growth in GDP per capita”: in dollars or in percent?

If you want to change anything, you can leave comments in the plan or provide feedback in the Claude Code panel, either in the “Tell Claude what to do instead” box or by clicking “No, keep planning” and asking Claude to revise the plan (top screenshot on the right).

For example, I noticed in the plan above that Claude implied the table could turn out better with gtExtras, but that it wouldn’t use it because it wasn’t installed. So I said “No, keep planning” and asked it to install the package and use it (bottom screenshot on the right).

When you’re happy with the plan, approve it, choosing the option to approve edits automatically, and let Claude get to work. When it’s done, open report.html (e.g. right-click it in the Explorer and open it in the Viewer, or in your browser).

Let’s look through the report. Are the plots and the table sensible? Below are some screenshots of the report I got, but your report may look different.

  • Table – version 1
  • Table – version 2
  • Plot ex. 1
  • Plot ex. 2
  • Plot ex. 3
  • Plot ex. 4
  • Plot ex. 5

Finally, let’s ask Claude for a change. I will go with interactive plots, but you can ask for any change you like. Interactive plots are another good fit: packages like ggiraph have their own functions and options you’d otherwise have to learn, while checking the result only takes some hovering and clicking.

Make one of the plots interactive with ggiraph, adding tooltips and hover effects

(As with countrycode, Claude should first ask to install ggiraph.)

For me, Claude made the life expectancy plot interactive. Hover over a point to see the country’s values, and to highlight all countries on the same continent:

Show the code 
library(tidyverse)
library(ggiraph)

factbook <- read_csv("factbook_tidy.csv")

# One colour-blind-safe colour per continent
continent_cols <- c(
  Africa = "#D55E00",
  Americas = "#0072B2",
  Asia = "#009E73",
  Europe = "#CC79A7",
  Oceania = "#E69F00"
)

# One row per country with the 2000 and 2015 life expectancy
life <- factbook |>
  filter(
    indicator == "Life expectancy at birth, total (years)",
    year %in% c(2000, 2015)
  ) |>
  select(country, continent, year, value) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = value, names_prefix = "y") |>
  drop_na(y2000, y2015) |>
  mutate(
    tip = str_glue(
      "{country} ({continent})\n2000: {round(y2000, 1)} years\n2015: {round(y2015, 1)} years\nGain: {round(y2015 - y2000, 1)} years"
    )
  )

p_life <- ggplot(life, aes(y2000, y2015, colour = continent)) +
  geom_abline(
    slope = 1,
    intercept = 0,
    linetype = "dashed",
    colour = "grey40"
  ) +
  # data_id = continent: hovering one country highlights its whole continent
  geom_point_interactive(
    aes(tooltip = tip, data_id = continent),
    alpha = 0.8,
    size = 2.2
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = continent_cols, name = NULL) +
  labs(
    title = "Almost every country gained years of life",
    subtitle = "Dashed line = no change",
    x = "Life expectancy in 2000 (years)",
    y = "Life expectancy in 2015 (years)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )

girafe(
  ggobj = p_life,
  width_svg = 8,
  height_svg = 5,
  options = list(
    opts_hover(css = "fill-opacity:1; stroke-opacity:1; stroke-width:2px;"),
    opts_hover_inv(css = "opacity:0.2;"),
    opts_tooltip(
      css = "background:white; color:#222; padding:6px 8px;
                        border-radius:4px; box-shadow:0 1px 4px #0006;"
    )
  )
)

Exercise: Ohio State branding with a _brand.yml

brand.yml is a format to define your organization’s colors, fonts, and logos in a single file, _brand.yml, which Quarto (and Shiny) then use to style your documents.

A _brand.yml is automatically used by Quarto to define the overall look (fonts, colors of headings and links) of the report, but it (understandably) won’t style the plots and tables according to brand colors — that’s where Claude comes in.

Download this _brand.yml for Ohio State and save it in your codeclub-claude folder as _brand.yml (rename it if your browser saved it as osu_brand.yml). Alternatively, create the file yourself and paste in the contents from the box below. Then, have a look at the file.

  Click to see the contents of _brand.yml 
_brand.yml
# A _brand.yml for Ohio State-styled Quarto documents and Shiny apps
# Colors follow OSU's brand palette; fonts are freely available Google Fonts
# stand-ins for OSU's Buckeye Sans/Serif

meta:
  name:
    short: Ohio State
    full: The Ohio State University
  link: https://www.osu.edu

color:
  palette:
    scarlet: "#BA0C2F"
    gray: "#A7B1B7"
    dark-gray: "#3F4443"
    light-gray: "#F2F2F2"
    black: "#212325"
    white: "#FFFFFF"
  foreground: black
  background: white
  primary: scarlet
  secondary: dark-gray
  light: light-gray
  dark: dark-gray

typography:
  fonts:
    - family: Source Sans 3
      source: google
      weight: [400, 600, 700]
      style: [normal, italic]
    - family: Source Serif 4
      source: google
      weight: [600, 700]
    - family: Source Code Pro
      source: google
  base:
    family: Source Sans 3
    line-height: 1.5
  headings:
    family: Source Serif 4
    weight: 700
    color: scarlet
  monospace: Source Code Pro
  link:
    color: scarlet

In a new conversation, ask Claude:

Use the colors from @_brand.yml in the plots and tables of @report.qmd where appropriate

This is a good place to practice with adding files as context using @:

The Ohio State colors are quite limiting, consisting only of scarlet and shades of gray, so they may not work well for all plots and tables, hence the “where appropriate” hedge in the prompt.

Then, check how it did!

  Click to see what I got

Probably for the best, Claude decided to keep its main color palette the way it was, but use Ohio State colors for plot titles, labels, and so on:

Overall, this report doesn’t necessarily look better, I think — but you may simply want or have to use the branding anyway:

At any rate, the table came out quite nice:

NoteHaving Claude create a _brand.yml (Click to expand)

So how do you get a _brand.yml in the first place? You can just ask Claude! For example:

Create a _brand.yml for Ohio State, using scarlet #BA0C2F and gray #A7B1B7

Or point it to your lab’s or organization’s style guide (e.g., a PDF).

7.4 A small Shiny app

Shiny lets you build interactive web apps (dropdowns, sliders, plots and tables that update as you click) using only R or Python code. Shiny apps are perhaps the best example of a “hard to write, easy to check” task: they need a lot of boilerplate code with an unusual “reactive” logic that many people find hard to learn and rarely write often enough to remember. But to check the result, you just run the app and click around to see whether it does what you want.

In a new conversation, submit:

Create a small Shiny app app.R using bslib and our _brand.yml, where I can pick a country and an indicator, and see a line plot over 2000-2015 and a wide-format gt table of the values. Keep it under 100 lines.

Because of our CLAUDE.md instruction, Claude should not try to run the app itself. Instead, open app.R and click the Run App button at the top of the editor: the app will open in Positron’s Viewer pane. It may look something like this:

If you have time, ask for a follow-up change:

Add the option to select a second country to compare against

Also try to “break” the app: pick a country and indicator combination for which there is no data. What happens? If the app shows an error or an empty plot, ask Claude to handle this better.

7.5 More ideas to try

7.5.1 With this data

Some other examples of good tasks for Claude Code that are not too expensive:

  • Parameterized report: “Turn report.qmd into a one-page country profile with the country as a parameter, and render it for Ghana, Peru, and Armenia”
  • Slides: “Turn the report into a short Quarto revealjs slide deck with the same branding”
  • Translate code: “Rewrite this to use base R code instead” or “Translate R code to Python”
  • A map: “Using factbook_tidy.csv, make a world map of life expectancy in 2015, colored by country”
  • Code review: “Review clean-factbook.R for bugs, unclear code, and hard-coded values”
  • README: “Write a README.md that explains what this project does and how to reproduce the results”

7.5.2 Other

Not for now, but here are some other things you can try with Claude Code:

  • Troubleshoot your code, software installations, and so on
  • Turn your code into a package
  • Document your code or write a tutorial based on your code
  • Draft Methods bullet points from code
  • Review Word documents: Claude can read and edit Word documents, and it can do so with Tracked Changes and leave comments, just like a human reviewer. You can also add so-called “skills” to Claude, such as ones to review scientific manuscripts (example repo).

8 Appendix

8.1 Agents fill up the context window quickly

A model’s context window holds everything in the conversation, and performance degrades as it fills up. With an agent, this happens much faster than with a chatbot: every file Claude reads and every command output it sees goes into the context too. To see how full the context window is, type /context in the prompt box.

8.2 Start fresh often

Today, we’ve started a new conversation for each new task. That’s a good habit: Claude can get confused when you switch topics within a conversation, and a long conversation is slower and more expensive, because with every new prompt, the entire conversation is sent to the model again.

To make re-sending the conversation cheaper, the part that hasn’t changed since the previous turn is cached, and cached tokens cost only about one tenth of the regular price. However, with an API key like ours, the cache expires after only 5 minutes without activity — the clock icon in the prompt box shows how much time is left. After that, your next message reprocesses the entire conversation at the full price. So when you come back to a long conversation after a break, consider starting a new one instead.

If you do want to continue a long conversation, type /compact in the prompt box: Claude then replaces the conversation so far with a summary, which frees up context.

8.3 Cost

Every token costs money, and your API key has a limited budget. To see an estimate of what the current conversation has cost so far, type /usage in the prompt box.

To keep costs down:

  • Stick to Sonnet at Medium effort (the default in your settings file).
  • Start fresh for each new task, and point Claude to specific files.
  • Don’t ask Claude to “read” or “analyze” large data files: have it write code that does the analysis instead.
  • For general questions, like explaining a concept or a function, a browser-based chat (e.g. Gemini or Copilot through your OSU account) works just as well and doesn’t use your API key’s budget.
NoteAPI pricing vs. personal subscriptions (Click to expand)

Paying per token through an API key, as we do here, is much more expensive than a personal subscription to a service like Claude, which has a fixed monthly fee. A day of heavy agentic coding through an API can easily cost more than a month’s subscription. However, personal accounts are not approved for institutional data, which includes your unpublished research data.

8.4 Good habits when working with an agent

Getting good help

  • Be explicit. Point Claude to the relevant files, and put your conventions and rules in CLAUDE.md.
  • Start fresh for each new task, and keep conversations focused.
  • Use Plan mode for bigger tasks, and review the plan before Claude starts.

Checking and keeping the results

  • You own the result. Read every proposed edit and command before approving it.
  • Verify, don’t trust. When Claude says something “works”, that may be a prediction rather than a test result. Run the code yourself, and check results independently.
  • Results should come from code you can rerun. Let Claude help you write code that you review, run, and keep; don’t rely on numbers or conclusions it only reports in the chat.
  • Commit before, review after. Use Git so that you can see and undo what Claude changed (Positron’s Source Control view makes this easy).
  • Keep a record of how you used AI, which journals increasingly ask you to disclose (see the box below).
NoteDocumenting your AI use (Click to expand)

Save your conversations
Claude saves your conversations automatically, but not in your project, and in a format that’s not easy to read. To save a conversation in your project as a plain-text file, type /export in the prompt box.

Let Claude keep a diary
For a concise overview, you can let Claude keep a diary of key findings and decisions, by adding something like this to your CLAUDE.md:

CLAUDE.md (excerpt)
## AI diary

- After completing a task, add an entry at the bottom of `doc/ai-diary.md`
  with the date, what I asked for, which files you created or changed,
  and any key decisions (including alternatives that were rejected)
- Keep entries short

Bonus exercise: Fix a script

The script penguin_summary.R should compute the number of penguins and their mean body mass, for Adelie and Gentoo penguins, but it has two problems.

  Click to see the script’s code 
penguin_summary.R
# Summarize body mass for Adelie and Gentoo penguins
# (uses the penguins data that is built into R 4.5.0 and later)

library(tidyverse)

# Keep only Adelie and Gentoo penguins
two_species <- penguins |>
  filter(species == c("Adelie", "Gentoo"))

# Number of penguins and mean body mass per species
two_species |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarize(
    n = n(),
    mean_mass_g = mean(body_mass)
  )

  1. Open the script and run it. What’s wrong with the output?

      Click to see the output

     
    # A tibble: 2 × 3
species     n mean_mass_g
<fct>   <int>       <dbl>
1 Adelie     76       3407.
2 Gentoo     62         NA

  2. Start a new conversation, and with the script open, ask Claude:

    Explain what this script does

    Does its explanation match your own understanding?

    It may well have pointed out one or two problems with the script, and if it did, it may have offered to fix them. If so, affirm that you want it to fix the problem(s) it found.

  3. In case Claude didn’t note the problem that produces the NA in the output, ask:

    I ran this and the mean body mass for Gentoo is NA. Fix it.

    It should be able to identify and fix this problem, and if it hadn’t already fixed the other problem, it may fix that too.

  4. Run the script yourself. If the results are like this, the problems are fixed:

    # A tibble: 2 × 3
species     n mean_mass_g
<fct>   <int>       <dbl>
1 Adelie    152       3701.
2 Gentoo    124       5076.

    If not, ask Claude to look for another problem.

Click here for the solution

The script contains two errors:

  • mean() returns NA when there are any missing values, unless you use na.rm = TRUE. This is easy to spot, because the output contains an NA.

  • species == c("Adelie", "Gentoo") does not check whether species is one of these two values. Instead, R “recycles” the two-element vector along all rows, comparing row 1 to "Adelie", row 2 to "Gentoo", row 3 to "Adelie", and so on. As a result, about half of the Adelie and Gentoo penguins are silently dropped. The fix is to use %in% instead of ==.

The second error is the more dangerous one, because it silently produces wrong results: there is no error or warning, and the output looks plausible. Before the fix, the script reports 76 Adelie and 62 Gentoo penguins, whereas there are 152 and 124.

two_species <- penguins |>
  filter(species %in% c("Adelie", "Gentoo"))

two_species |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarize(
    n = n(),
    mean_mass_g = mean(body_mass, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

Did Claude catch the second error? It may have noticed it while reading the script, after running it and seeing suspicious counts, or not at all. This shows why code that runs without errors still needs to be checked, whether you or Claude wrote or fixed it.

Back to top

Footnotes

  1. Positron does make it possible to expose the same functionality for Claude Code, but that requires some setup and I have not yet tried that.↩︎

  2. Posit Assistant can also use an API key, but as mentioned above, its authentication sometimes acts up.↩︎

  3. All of this can also be done without code, in a perhaps more intuitive way, but the interface will differ between computers, so this is less likely to fail here.↩︎

  4. The previous view, of the initial script, was also a diff, but this wasn’t as obvious because there were only additions↩︎

  5. Click the x to remove it.↩︎

item.title: AI-assisted plotting with R and Positron
item.dc:creator: Jessica Cooperstone
Jelmer Poelstra
item.description:
1 Introduction

1.1 What we’ll cover

Developments in generative artificial intelligence (AI) using large language models (LLMs) is revolutizing the way the people code. We have covered in many past Code Clubs how to use ggplot2 in R to make the plots of your dreams, and today we are going to talk about aiding that process using AI.

By the end of the session, you should be more comfortable with using AI to aid in your plotting. Specifically, we’ll cover:

  • The basics of ggplot2 syntax
  • Using AI to make a simple plot
  • Using prompts to refine that plot more
  • Prompting to make a much more complicated figure

Discussion

  • Do you currently use AI to help with your plotting?
  • If yes, how do you integrate AI into your workflow?
  • Do you consider yourself familiar with the basics ggplot2?

1.2 Before we start

We are going to be working in Positron for the rest of the semester. If you haven’t done so already, please:

  1. Install Positron: download the appropriate installer from the download page, and run it. There are installers for Windows, macOS, and Linux.

  2. Make sure you have a recent R (4.4.0 or higher) installed; Positron does not come with its own copy of R.

ImportantUsing an OSU-managed computer and have no admin rights?

You should still be able to install Positron, just do so at the user level rather than system-wide.

On a Mac, this involves dragging the Positron app into your User Applications folder, /Users/<username>/Applications (i.e. this Applications folder is in the same parent folder as your Documents, Downloads, and Desktop folder).

On Windows, the Positron installer has a “User install” option. Look for a checkbox or dropdown labeled “Install for me only” (vs. “for all users”) during setup — that keeps the install in your user profile without needing admin rights.

2 Getting started

Go ahead and start Positron! It should look something like this:

2.1 Opening a folder (replaces RStudio Projects)

On the left side of the Positron window, you should see something similar to what’s shown in the screenshot on the right, prompting you to open a folder.

“Opening a folder” is Positron’s equivalent of opening an RStudio Project. The idea is the same: a folder is a self-contained workspace, and opening it sets your working directory and gives you a fresh R session.

But instead of requiring the special .Rproj file that is created when you make an RStudio Project, Positron simply treats any folder you open as a project.

Let’s open a new folder for today’s session:

  1. You can use the folder you created last month when you learned about Positron from Jelmer, or you can create a new folder to use today. You can create it in any way, such as with your computer’s File Explorer / Finder.

    I would suggest putting this folder within a folder for Code Club, for example: Documents > codeclub > 26-au (or put another way: ~/Documents/codeclub/26-au). Again, it would be fine to use the same folder from our August session.

  2. Open this folder in Positron by clicking the Open Folder button shown above1.

  3. Positron will reload and ask whether you want to trust the folder. Click Yes, I trust the authors and optionally check the box above it.

Why are Projects or open folders needed? These encourage good practices:

  • Keep each research project in its own self-contained folder
  • Use paths relative to the folder root, not absolute paths
  • Avoid using setwd()

They also make a lot of Positron’s features work better, such as the Explorer, Search, and version control support.

2.2 Setting up Positron to use GitHub Copilot with Posit Assistant

You can set up Posit Assistant to work with a variety of different LLMs. Today we will set it up for using GitHub Copilot.

The two main AI tools we have are:

  1. Code completions where you get AI suggested completions as you type
  2. Agentic chat using Posit Assistant where you can both get code suggestions and have the agent run the code for you.

2.2.1 Get a GitHub account if you don’t have one

In order to use GitHub Copilot with Posit Assistant, you must have a GitHub account.

Create a GitHub account by going to github.com/join.

  • You will have to link to an email address. You can use your OSU email or a personal one, it doesn’t matter.
  • You will have to pick a username. Some advice for picking a username:
    • Incorporate your actual name - it’s useful for seeing who you are
    • Pick a username you’d be comfortable with an employer seeing
    • Shorter is better
    • Recommend to use all lower case letters
    • Your username can be changed but its annoying so try and get it right the first time
Tip

You can sign up for GitHub education with your OSU email by confirming your status as a student GitHub Education page.

Anyone with a GitHub account will be automatically enrolled in the free GitHub Copilot plan, which has a limit of 2,000 code completions per month and ~50 chat requests. That’s not enough for most people to use GitHub Copilot in a sustained way — but as students and teachers/faculty, we can get additional free access after applying for it. In summary (see also this GitHub page):

Plan Free for whom How to get it Code completions Chat requests
Free Everyone Automatically 2,000 per month ~50
Student Students Apply for education benefits Unlimited 200
Pro Teachers/Faculty Apply for education benefits Unlimited 1,500

To apply for educational benefits, the following link will work for teachers/faculty and students alike — just select the appropriate option in the form:

  1. Go to https://github.com/settings/education/benefits.

  2. Click “Start an application”:

  3. Fill out the form as needed. (You will likely need a document that proves your current status at the university.)

2.2.2 Set your LLM provider to GitHub Copilot

In order to set up the Posit Assistant for AI-assisted plotting, you will need to configure the Posit Assistant extension. We will configure it to use GitHub Copilot.

NoteWant to set up with a different LLM?

Jelmer has created some intructions for how to set up Claude Code using your OSU LiteLLM API

To do that, call up your Command Palette (Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+P), and we are going to configure which LLMs our Posit Assistant can use. Type in “Authentication: Configure Language Model Providers” and select it.

NoteDon’t see Authentication: Configure Language Model Providers as an option?(Click to expand)

This may be because:

  • You have an old version of Positron installed. Go to the Positron site and download/install the newest version.
  • You don’t have the Posit Assistant extension installed.
    1. Open the Extensions view in Positron by clicking the Extension icon in the Activity Bar (the narrow leftmost sidebar).
    2. In the search box, start typing “Posit Assistant”
    3. Click Install on the “Posit Assistant” extension by Posit Software, PBC.

This will prompt opening a new window where you can select which LLM provider you want to use. There are more options than what you can see in the screenshot below.

Today we are going to select GitHub Copilot, which is free to use for students and academics. You will need to have a GitHub account and sign in to GitHub Copilot. Go ahead and click the orange Connect Positron to GitHub Copilot. A new pop up with open that says “The extension ‘Authentication’ wants to sign in using GitHub. Click the blue Allow. This will open a new browser window where you can sign in to GitHub and authorize Posit Assistant to use GitHub Copilot.

Next you will get popup that includes a code for authenticating in your browser. You can click Copy & Continue to Browser and the 8 digit code will be added to your clipboard and a browser will open.

You will need to be logged into a GitHub account to do this - you can see that mine shows up below. You might also have the option here to log in.

Now you can authorize your device to use GitHub Copilot with Positron. Your code should be ready in your clipboard, you can paste it here using (Cmd/Ctrl+V)

Now you can authorize VS code to access items within your GitHub account. Yours might look different than mine depending on what groups you are involved with. You can press the green button to Authorize Visual-Studio-Code.

Now you should be connected.

NoteGetting a popup that you have not finished authorizing GitHub? There are some instructions below to authorize by creating a Personal Access Token (PAT) (Click to expand)

While preparing the material for today’s session, I set up GitHub Copilot in Positron about 5 times. Sometimes when I would set up, I would get the pop up on the bottom right of my Positron window:

If you get this prompt, you can click the orange Yes. This will initiate a new popup that asks if you want to Continue to GitHub to create a Personal Access Token (PAT). You can click the blue Continue to GitHub.

You should next get a popup asking “Do you want Positron to open the external website?” and you can click the blue Open.

This will bring you to your GitHub account online where you can create a Personal Access Token (PAT). You can do this with all the defaults, and you will need to set an expiration date. GitHub recommends you set at 30 days but you can do longer. If you scroll to the bottom of hte page, you will find a green Generate token button - go ahead and click that.

Your PAT will then be created and you can see it. Be sure to copy this, and I like to save this token also in my password manager. Then you can navigate back to Postrion where there should be a prompt asking you for this PAT.

Paste your PAT and press Enter. You should now be connected to GitHub Copilot through Positron.

2.3 Starting an R session

Near the top-right corner of the Positron window is the so-called interpreter picker, which lets you choose which installation of R (or Python) to use for your session.

If Positron found your R installation, it may have started a session already — then it would look similar to what’s shown in the screenshot on the right (with the R version number corresponding to what you have installed).

3 Re-familiarizing ourself with ggplot2 syntax

Perhaps it is possible now to use AI to make your plots without understanding any ggplot2 or R syntax, but I do think it is much easier, and you’ll have a better time if you understand the basics.

3.1 Installing and loading the tidyverse

Before we start going through the syntactical basics, we need to have ggplot2 installed in R. If you were here last time, you’ll already have the tidyverse (and ggplot2 is one of the packages contain in this meta-package), but if you weren’t then you will need to first download it using install.packages(). Then you can load the tidyverse by calling it with the function library().

library(tidyverse)
TipPrefer that your output be displayed in the source editor?

If you liked that output would be shown in the source editor, directly below code, like you might be used to in RStudio, you can enable inline output by turning on quarto.inlineOutput.enabled.

We are going to use the penguins dataset that comes preloaded with base R. If you want to see all of these datasets, you can run library(help = "datasets")

glimpse(datasets::penguins)
Rows: 344
Columns: 8
$ species     <fct> Adelie, Adelie, Adelie, Adelie, Adelie, Adelie, Adelie, Ad…
$ island      <fct> Torgersen, Torgersen, Torgersen, Torgersen, Torgersen, Tor…
$ bill_len    <dbl> 39.1, 39.5, 40.3, NA, 36.7, 39.3, 38.9, 39.2, 34.1, 42.0, …
$ bill_dep    <dbl> 18.7, 17.4, 18.0, NA, 19.3, 20.6, 17.8, 19.6, 18.1, 20.2, …
$ flipper_len <int> 181, 186, 195, NA, 193, 190, 181, 195, 193, 190, 186, 180,…
$ body_mass   <int> 3750, 3800, 3250, NA, 3450, 3650, 3625, 4675, 3475, 4250, …
$ sex         <fct> male, female, female, NA, female, male, female, male, NA, …
$ year        <int> 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007…

I am clipping below a bit of the []ggplot2 cheatsheet](https://github.com/rstudio/cheatsheets/blob/main/data-visualization.pdf) to see how the developesr explain the basis of plotting.

The general syntax is like this:

data |> # start with dataframe and pipe to ggplot()
  ggplot(aes(x = _x-variable_, # inside aes set variables mapped to visual aspects
             y = _y-variable_, 
             color = _color-variable)) + 
    geom_*() + # add a geometry - the type of plot
    scale_*() + # set how data maps to visual aspects 
    theme_*() + # adjust the overall look of the plot
    labs() + # add labels - title, axes, legend

You can find the full ggplot2 cheatsheet also for reference.

4 Simple plots

Let’s start with with asking the Posit Assistant for help with a plot. Let’s ask for:

“Create a plot using the penguins dataset that plots flipper length versus bill length.”

When I did this for the first time, I got a pop up asking “Can Posit Assistant use executeCode?” This would mean that the Posit Assistant would like to actually run this code, versus just provide the code for me to run.

I am going to click Allow and see what happens. Alternatively you could click Deny and the Posit Assistant will provide you with code that you can copy and paste into your script or .qmd file to run.

When I do this, I get the following code, which I can see in my console:

library(ggplot2)
library(palmerpenguins)

Attaching package: 'palmerpenguins'
The following objects are masked from 'package:datasets':

    penguins, penguins_raw
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = flipper_length_mm)) +
  geom_point()
Warning: Removed 2 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_point()`).

There are a few things to note here, Posit AI has:

  1. loaded the packages it needs to run the code its specified.
  2. decided that the data we want is in the package palmerpenguins even though I was expecting it to pull from the base R penguins dataset. This is fine, but it is something to be aware of as these two datasets are not identical. For example, the variable names in palmerpenguins::penguins are different than in datasets::penguins.
  3. not used the pipe |> operator which is a more modern way to write code that is considered best practice. This approach is fine but it is something to be aware of.

While this is a very good start, let’s see if different prompting can get us a different result. I am now going to ask for:

“Create a plot using the penguins dataset embedded in base R that plots flipper length versus bill length. Use the pipe operator and add code annotations so I can follow what each line is doing.”

When I do this, I get the following code:

# Load the penguins dataset from datasets package
datasets::penguins |>
  # Extract the columns we need for plotting
  (\(d) data.frame(
    bill_length = d$bill_length_mm,
    flipper_length = d$flipper_length_mm
  ))() |>
  # Remove rows with missing values
  (\(d) d[complete.cases(d), ])() |>
  # Create the plot with bill_length on x-axis and flipper_length on y-axis
  with(plot(
    x = bill_length,
    y = flipper_length,
    main = "Penguin Measurements",
    xlab = "Bill Length (mm)",
    ylab = "Flipper Length (mm)",
    pch = 19,
    col = rgb(0, 0, 0, 0.6)
  ))

This code has a number of problems, is actually worse than my first attempt, and does not work for me at all. I notice a few problems:

  1. I asked for the penguins dataset which is a part of base R, and Posit AI has given me a fully base R plot, which is not what I want. I can change my prompt to fix this problem.
  2. Because the assistant thinks I want a base R plot, this leads to addition code which is fully not necessary. There are some steps that aim to extract the columns from the data, which is needed for base R plotting, but this is also done incorrectly. The code we’ve received is (trying) to extract bill_length_mm and flipper_length_mm from penguins but those are not the correct variable names.

Let’s try a new prompt:

“Create a plot using the data datasets::penguins using ggplot2 that plots flipper length versus bill length. Use the pipe operator and add code annotations so I can follow what each line is doing.”

Now I get this code:

library(ggplot2)

# Load the penguins dataset from the datasets package
datasets::penguins |>
  # Initialize ggplot with bill_length_mm on x-axis and flipper_length_mm on y-axis
  ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = flipper_length_mm)) +
  # Add a scatter plot layer with semi-transparent points
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 3) +
  # Add labels for the axes and title
  labs(
    title = "Penguin Measurements",
    x = "Bill Length (mm)",
    y = "Flipper Length (mm)"
  )

Better but still I have the wrong variable names. What if I try and give the prompt information about my dataset? I am going to paste the output of glimpse(datasets::penguins) into the end of my prompt such that the AI can see exactly what my data looks like.

Create a plot using the data datasets::penguins using ggplot2 that plots flipper length versus bill length. Use the pipe operator and add code annotations so I can follow what each line is doing. I am pasting below the output of glimpse(datasets::penguins) so you can see what the data looks like.

glimpse(datasets::penguins)
Rows: 344
Columns: 8
$ species     <fct> Adelie, Adelie, Adelie, Adelie, Adelie, Adelie, Adelie, Ad…
$ island      <fct> Torgersen, Torgersen, Torgersen, Torgersen, Torgersen, Tor…
$ bill_len    <dbl> 39.1, 39.5, 40.3, NA, 36.7, 39.3, 38.9, 39.2, 34.1, 42.0, …

$ sex         <fct> male, female, female, NA, female, male, female, male, NA, …
$ year        <int> 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007…

Ok now I am getting a functional plot:

library(ggplot2)

# Load the penguins dataset from the datasets package
datasets::penguins |>
  # Initialize ggplot with bill_len on x-axis and flipper_len on y-axis
  ggplot(aes(x = bill_len, y = flipper_len)) +
  # Add a scatter plot layer with semi-transparent points
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 3) +
  # Add labels for the axes and title
  labs(
    title = "Penguin Measurements",
    x = "Bill Length (mm)",
    y = "Flipper Length (mm)"
  )
Warning: Removed 2 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_point()`).

I have gotten a little bit more than I asked for - Posit AI decided that the points should be better (size = 3) and be a bit transparent (alpha = 0.6) which I think is ok. I also have gotten x- and y-axis labels along with a title even though I didn’t ask for that.

4.1 Exercise: Try it yourself

  1. Try on your own to prompt Posit AI to make you a new plot with this same data. Play around and then we will all share our experiences.

  2. What have you learned about what makes a successful prompt?

5 More complicated plots/involved requests

We’ve done some simple plots but what if we want to make something much more complicated? We could think about this in two ways:

  1. We could ask for a much more customized plot
  2. We could see how well we think Posit AI can select a visualization tool without providing that information explicitly.

Let’s pick a more involved dataset, one we’ve used in Code Club before to have more variables to interrogate. The data we are going to download can be found here, though I have saved the file, added it to our Code Club Github, and included some code below for you to download it.

item.description:
1 Introduction

1.1 What we’ll cover

Every Code Club session so far has used RStudio. Today we’ll spend the session in a different program: Positron, a newer data science IDE from Posit, the same company that makes RStudio.

By the end of the session, you should be able to open your own work in Positron, find your way around, and decide for yourself whether you want to keep using it. Specifically, we’ll cover:

  • Installing Positron
  • Positron’s open folder feature
  • Running code and the Command Palette
  • Touring the interface
  • Exploring data with the Data Explorer and more
  • Customizing Positron

1.2 Why is there a new IDE?

Basically, Posit wanted better support for other programming languages, particularly Python, alongside R. This turned out to be harder to retrofit into RStudio than to start fresh, so they created a new IDE: Positron.

Positron is built on Code OSS, the open-source base of Microsoft’s popular general-purpose code editor, Visual Studio Code (VS Code). It adds data science features that RStudio has but VS Code does not, such as a Variables pane, a Plots pane, and a Data Explorer.

Discussion

  • Which languages do you use besides R — Python, Bash, SQL, none?
  • Has anyone tried Positron already? Did you stick with it?
  • Do you consider yourself familiar with the basics of RStudio?

1.3 Why should you consider switching?

If you use Python alongside R, or are already familiar with VS Code, Positron is a natural choice and I’d strongly recommend switching.

If you use R only, you may not need to switch, but should still consider it, because:

  • Future new features: While Posit has committed to maintaining and updating RStudio, major new features are now going to Positron first. And some features may never make it to RStudio, because Positron is more adaptable.

  • AI support: This is much more flexible in Positron, where you can connect to different model providers and subscriptions, and even use Claude Code. In RStudio, you can only use AI via a Posit AI subscription. We’ll demonstrate using AI assistance in Positron in the next session!

  • Customization: Positron is more customizable than RStudio.

And two more minor points:

  • Data Explorer: Positron’s Data Explorer can open data files (CSV, Excel, etc.) directly, without having to load them in R at all.

  • Remote connections: a niche feature, but one that was important to me. Positron can connect to the Ohio Supercomputer Center, or any other remote server. That isn’t possible with RStudio — and while you can run RStudio directly at OSC through OSC OnDemand, that has its downsides. (Happy to expand on this for any OSC users!)

1.4 Before we start

If you haven’t done so already, please:

  1. Install Positron: download the appropriate installer from the download page, and run it. There are installers for Windows, macOS, and Linux.

  2. Make sure you have a recent R (4.4.0 or higher) installed; Positron does not come with its own copy of R.

ImportantUsing an OSU-managed computer and have no admin rights?

You should still be able to install Positron, just do so at the user level rather than system-wide.

On a Mac, this involves dragging the Positron app into your User Applications folder, /Users/<username>/Applications (i.e. this Applications folder is in the same parent folder as your Documents, Downloads, and Desktop folders).

On Windows, the Positron installer has a “User install” option. Look for a checkbox or dropdown labeled “Install for me only” (vs. “for all users”) during setup — that keeps the install in your user profile without needing admin rights.

2 Getting started

Go ahead and start Positron! It should look something like this:

2.1 Opening a folder (replaces RStudio Projects)

On the left side of the Positron window, you should see something similar to what’s shown in the screenshot on the right, prompting you to open a folder.

“Opening a folder” is Positron’s equivalent of opening an RStudio Project. The idea is the same: a folder is a self-contained workspace, and opening it sets your working directory and gives you a fresh R session.

But instead of requiring the special .Rproj file that is created when you make an RStudio Project, Positron simply treats any folder you open as a project.

Let’s create and open a new folder for today’s session:

  1. Create a new folder on your computer. You can create it in any way, such as with your computer’s File Explorer / Finder. I would suggest putting this folder within a folder for Code Club, for example: Documents > codeclub > positron (or put another way: ~/Documents/codeclub/positron).

  2. Open your new folder in Positron by clicking the Open Folder button shown above1.

  3. Positron will reload and ask whether you want to trust the folder. Click Yes, I trust the authors and optionally check the box above it.

Why are Projects or open folders needed? These encourage good practices:

  • Keep each research project in its own self-contained folder
  • Use paths relative to the folder root, not absolute paths
  • Avoid using setwd()

They also make a lot of Positron’s features work better, such as the Explorer, Search, and version control support.

NoteMore on RStudio Projects vs. Positron folders

If you open a folder that already contains an .Rproj file, Positron simply ignores the file. So a folder can work as both an RStudio Project and a Positron workspace, which is perhaps handy while you’re trying Positron out.

The good thing about Positron’s mechanism is that you’re practically forced to use it, whereas in RStudio using Projects is easy to skip or not even know about.

2.2 Starting an R session

Near the top-right corner of the Positron window is the so-called interpreter picker, which lets you choose which installation of R (or Python) to use for your session.

If Positron found your R installation, it may have started a session already — in that case, it will look similar to what’s shown in the screenshot on the right (but with the R version number corresponding to what you have installed).

If not, click the picker, and choose your version of R (you may have to click New Console Session before you see the available options):

NoteMore on R and Python sessions in Positron

The picker lists every interpreter Positron can find, which could include several versions of R and especially Python. Two nice features of Positron:

  • Switching between R versions is a single click here, which is considerably easier than in RStudio.
  • You can also have several sessions running at once. Say, an R session and a Python session, or two R sessions on different R versions.

On the other hand, if you’re an R user only and have no need to switch between different R versions, you might prefer the simplicity of RStudio’s approach.

Once a session is running, the R Console works just like in RStudio. Try it:

# R is even better than AI and will consistently get this right! Impressive stuff.
1 + 1
[1] 2
head(iris)
  Sepal.Length Sepal.Width Petal.Length Petal.Width Species
1          5.1         3.5          1.4         0.2  setosa
2          4.9         3.0          1.4         0.2  setosa
3          4.7         3.2          1.3         0.2  setosa
4          4.6         3.1          1.5         0.2  setosa
5          5.0         3.6          1.4         0.2  setosa
6          5.4         3.9          1.7         0.4  setosa

Here’s what that will look like in Positron:

Exercise

A) Confirm your working directory

Confirm that opening a folder really did set your working directory: run getwd() and check that the path matches the folder you opened.

B) Try running two sessions

Start a second R session from the interpreter picker: click the picker, then New Console Session. (Most likely, you only have a single R version installed, and can pick the same version for the second session. If you have multiple, you can choose to use a different version for the second session.)

You should now have two Console sessions, which should look something like this — pay attention to the right-hand side:

Click on the second (bottom) session, and run:

x <- 1

Then switch back to the first session, and run:

x
Error:
! object 'x' not found

If you get the above error, that means the two sessions are independent: objects created in one session do not exist in the other.

2.3 Packages and a script

In the Exploring data section below, we’ll use the flights dataset from the nycflights13 package. This data frame has every flight that departed New York City in 2013. For now, we’ll get it installed and loaded, and will create a script to hold our code.

First, let’s install the two packages we’ll need, tidyverse and nycflights13:

install.packages("tidyverse")
install.packages("nycflights13")
TipAlready have these packages installed?

If you already have them or think you do, you can skip the installation step and try running the library() calls below directly. Alternatively, it won’t hurt to run the install.packages() calls again — R will simply check that you have the latest version and skip the installation if you do.

Now, let’s create a new R script:

  • Click File (or the “New” button) > New File..., then select “R File” (one of several ways to do this).

  • Save it right away (File > Save or Save As, or Cmd/Ctrl+S) in your current folder as explore.R.

I recommend that you add all the code below to this script, and run it from the script (instead of typing it into the console).

Load the two packages we’ll use:

library(tidyverse)

✔ forcats   1.0.1     ✔ stringr   1.6.0

✔ lubridate 1.9.5     ✔ tidyr     1.3.2
✔ purrr     1.2.2
